docs.title: My Note
docs.text:
Welcome to the documentation :) and thank you for checking out Media Journal! I won't repeat the readme description, but I will mention the main points again: I love this app, I will maintain it forever, it will always be completely free and it makes me happy if even one person enjoys it alongside me.

It's not the most advanced app, nor am I a senior developer, but I care about this app and I use it daily. I think that's worth something and that's why I got this far with it.

Maybe a senior developer who is nonchalant about their app would have been better, BUT if you are one of the few unlucky people who are looking for an app exactly like this, now you are stuck with me! >:) See ya in the trenches.

docs.title: How do I set it up?
docs.text: Go to the Setup Guides

docs.title: How it works
docs.text: On this page I will explain the high-level flow of the app and some details about how it operates behind the scenes.

docs.title: 1. Where the data comes from
docs.text:
The app gets data for media items (like titles, descriptions, covers and banners) as well as people and characters from separate external APIs:

  • TMDB for Movies, TV shows and people
  • AniList for Anime, Manga, characters and staff, including voice actors and original creators
  • IGDB for Games
  • OpenLibrary for Books
  • MusicBrainz for Music

Note: Music is special because we also fetch the YouTube URL of the song whenever we fetch a track. The YouTube video comes separately through a search and is not provided by MusicBrainz itself.

Note: OpenLibrary is slow compared to the rest of the APIs but I chose it because it is highly likely to last and stay free. This ties into the longevity of the app which I explain below.

docs.title: 2. Local Storage
docs.text:
After the data is fetched it is saved locally on your machine. You can then edit the items to add your own tracking data like notes and scores or even edit the metadata (the information received from the API).

Library records and app settings are stored in data/db.sqlite3, while downloaded and uploaded images live in media/. Some interface choices, such as view modes, the last search type and music player positions, are saved in the browser instead. Those choices can differ between browsers and devices.

The rest of the features in the app are built entirely around this concept of fetching and saving locally. The notable exception is the Community page which adds another layer of integration. It uses a Realtime Database from Firebase to store the data for posts and comments rather than saving it on your local machine.

CSV transfer is another way to add items to this same local library. It resolves IDs or searches for titles, lets you review the matches, then fetches the normal provider metadata and applies the fields you mapped from the file. It does not keep the library synced with the app you exported from.

docs.title: 3. Longevity and API Reliability
docs.text:
As the app stands right now it should work well for years to come. The only real issue that could break functionality is if the current APIs close down or become paid.

I chose the current selection of APIs because they have all lasted a long time and are widely used. There are really low chances of any of them disappearing anytime soon.

In the worst case scenario that one does disappear we just have to hope there will be a replacement at that time which is highly likely. Even in that scenario your existing items will be completely safe. Because all your data is saved locally an API shutting down won't delete your lists. We would just have to link our existing items to the new API and I would update the app's code to work with the new provider.

docs.title: How to use
docs.text: On this page I will describe how you can use the app and explain some of its meaningful functionalities and details.

docs.title: 1.1 Search and Discover
docs.text:
After you add your API keys you can start adding items. The search button is available on every page. On a media list or details page it automatically selects that media type. On other pages, like Home or Settings, it remembers the last type you used.

You can also change the media type using the dropdown attached to the search bar. Its options follow your navigation button order and leave out media types you have hidden in Settings.

Note: Live search is controlled per media type from Settings > Preferences > Live Search. Movies, TV shows and games have it enabled by default. Anime, manga, books and music start with it disabled to reduce API requests. You can always press Enter to search manually.

Alternatively you can open the discover page from the home page. There you can just hover over an item and press the plus button to quickly add it.

Discover has different sorting and filtering options for each media type. For games, the Free to Play filter can be combined with Top Rated or Upcoming, genres and any available release year filter.

When using the search bar, clicking on an item will open its details page where you can press the add to my list button.

docs.title: 1.2 Details Page
docs.text:
Each media type has different sections on its details page. You can rearrange them or hide them completely from Settings > Preferences > Details Page Sections.

If you want to see more details about an item you can press on More Information. I made this button load extra information through an on-demand API call so you always get the latest data. This way whenever you load a page for an item already in your list there are no automatic API calls. The app only fetches data when you actually want it.

Here are some notable sections:

docs.title: 1.2.1 Journal Section
docs.text:
In this section you can see and write Notes and Logs. Notes also appear in the edit modal and are supposed to be a single place where you keep general thoughts about your media. Logs on the other hand can only be created from the journal section. You can have multiple logs for an item which gives you more options to keep detailed and sectioned info.

Note: Both your notes and logs will appear under each media item when you use the Detailed List View on list pages.

docs.title: 1.2.2 Cast & Characters Section
docs.text:
Here you will see 8 people or characters by default and you can see the rest with the load more button. When you hover over them you can favorite or unfavorite using the heart icon. There is also a search button here to search for a specific person or character.

People come from TMDB or AniList. Voice actors on character pages and original creators under More Information for anime and manga are clickable too, so you can open their person page and favorite them.

docs.title: 1.2.3 Music Section
docs.text: In this section you can add YouTube URLs to link videos for a music item. Just note that only the video at the top of the list will be played in the built-in music player.

docs.title: 1.2.4 Screenshots Section
docs.text:
Games automatically come with some screenshots fetched from the API but you can also add your own. The ADD button puts your new screenshots after the existing ones. The SWAP button asks for confirmation before you choose replacement images, then replaces all existing screenshots and removes their favorites.

You can delete a single screenshot or choose Delete More in the confirmation popup to select several previews for deletion. This selection mode is available outside fullscreen. Use the star to favorite a screenshot; favorites have a golden border in the preview strip. Hover over the star to show the option to view only favorites.

The fullscreen button opens a larger viewer. Double-click the image to switch between that view and true fullscreen. Use the mouse wheel to zoom towards the pointer, drag to move a zoomed image, and use the left/right arrow keys to change screenshots. Autoplay is available too.

The download button saves the current screenshot, or the visible part when zoomed in. In either fullscreen view, hover over Download to choose a square or circular crop. Your browser's download settings still decide whether it asks where to save the file.

You can also drag the bottom-right corner of the preview strip down to see more thumbnails. Its height resets when you open the page again. The small bottom-left corner on the main image reveals the screenshot's added date when one is available.

docs.title: 1.3 Custom Media Items
docs.text:
If you cannot find the media you are looking for you can create a custom item. Just press the + button directly from the list page of the media type where you want it placed. This is also very useful if you want to add media types that are not officially supported like comics, podcasts or board games.

You can select one or more existing collections directly in the create modal, so you don't have to assign them afterwards.

Note: You can make a Collection of all your custom items of an unsupported type so it basically acts as a dedicated custom list.

docs.title: 1.4 Edit Item
docs.text:
After adding your items you can start editing them by pressing the ... button from the list pages or the history page. You can also press Edit Item directly from the details page.

Besides the default tracking fields you can enable additional ones from Settings > Preferences > Edit Modal Fields. Options like Activity Date, Repeats and Collections are disabled by default so they don't clutter the edit modal if you don't need them.

You can also use the small + next to progress on list pages while an item is Watching, Reading or Playing. It adds one episode or chapter, with separate episode and season controls in TV list views. Movies, games, books and music use a simple complete action instead of adding minutes, hours or pages. Reaching the known total marks the item as Completed without assigning a score.

Activity Date updates when you change both status and score, or when an item moves from Watching/Reading/Playing to Completed or Dropped even without a score change. This also applies when the progress + completes an item. A date you explicitly change in the edit modal takes priority.

docs.title: 1.4.1 Scoring System
docs.text:
The app lets you change your scoring system at any time. All score values are saved locally on a 1 to 100 scale. For example a 5 out of 10 gets saved as 50, 3 stars get saved as 60 and a neutral face gets saved as 50. Because everything is standardized behind the scenes you can change from one scoring system to another without breaking your existing ratings.

The 1–10 and star views round to whole numbers when displaying a score. More precise values, such as 25 from a CSV import, stay saved in the database even if the 1–10 view displays them as 3.

docs.title: 1.5 Edit Metadata
docs.text:
By going to the details page and clicking the Gear icon > Edit Metadata you can manually edit the data fetched from the API. This includes things like genres, creators, release dates and so on.

Note: Keep in mind that if you ever press Refresh Data from the gear menu the app will fetch from the API again and your custom metadata will be overwritten.

docs.title: 1.6 Refresh Data
docs.text:
In Settings > Refresh > Refresh Data you can refresh all items or choose specific media types and fields (like genres, creators etc). This is sometimes more useful and convenient than manually refreshing data one by one on the details page. It is especially useful when I update the app and add a new field. For example when I added the Genres field all existing items needed to be refreshed to populate that field with data from the API.

Note: Some APIs are slower than others during this process because of their call limits or infrastructure speed.

docs.title: 1.7 Music Player
docs.text:
You can start the music player using the ♪ button on the home page when you have favorited at least 1 song. There is also a similar button that starts the player on the music list page. When the music player is started from the home page it will play only your favorited songs in a random order. The one started from the list page will play the songs from your currently selected status (All, Completed, Dropped etc) in a random order.

If you want to play a specific song you can hover over a music card and press the ▶ button, or use the play button on its row in a list view. This will play the selected song and continue with the songs next to it in their current order.

The player has small, medium, fullscreen and pop-out modes. In the small modes you can drag it using the grab areas over the video, leaving the center and YouTube controls available. Your mode and position are remembered in the browser. The history panel starts closed unless you choose to open it.

For uninterrupted playback while navigating, use the pop-out button that appears when you hover over the small/medium mode control. It opens the player in a separate window, which keeps playing while you browse the main app. Its size and position are remembered too, although the browser may adjust where it opens. The button beside X in that window brings it back into the page.

Note: The in-page player still reloads when you navigate to another page. Pop-out mode avoids that without needing to rebuild the app as a single page app. It is a normal browser window, so it does not stay on top of other windows automatically.

docs.title: 2. Main Pages & Features
docs.text: Now that you have your media items and your lists are growing here are some useful pages and functionalities you can use.

docs.title: 2.1 Home Page
docs.text:
The home page has multiple sections for favorites, stats, activity history, collections and upcoming releases.

Note: If you press on the Stats or Activity History titles they will swap to show Collections and Upcoming Releases instead. Your choice remains saved locally so you can leave them the way you prefer. Also if you press on any favorites section title (e.g. Movies, People etc) it will open the favorites page with that section at the top.

docs.title: 2.1.1 Stats Section
docs.text: This section shows the amount of media items you have and meaningful stats about them like days watched and days played. To make the page load faster I simplified how days watched is calculated the same way other sites do it. Rather than getting the exact length of each individual movie, TV show or anime I multiply them by an average value. I use 90 minutes per movie, 40 minutes per TV show episode and 24 minutes per anime episode. When your lists have hundreds or thousands of media items these average values are accurate enough so it's good enough.

docs.title: 2.1.2 Collections Section
docs.text: Here you can see your top 10 collections and quickly access the collections page using the arrow button.

docs.title: 2.1.3 Activity History Section
docs.text: Here you can see an activity graph that shows items you modified or added by activity date per day for the past 24 weeks (about 5.5 months). Under it you will find the latest media items and how long ago they were updated. You can also find the Media History button here which redirects you to the History page.

docs.title: 2.1.4 Upcoming Releases Section
docs.text:
Here you can view the latest releases in tiles for one week ahead and from the last week. It also shows the 12 newest upcoming releases and how long it is until they release. From here you can access the calendar page through the Calendar button.

Note: When you swap from activity history to upcoming releases the data for the calendar refreshes automatically and the tiles are populated so you don't have to go to the calendar page every time to get updates.

docs.title: 2.1.5 Favorites Section
docs.text: Each favorites section shows up to 25 of your media items, people or characters. You can reorder items on the favorites page if you want different ones to show up here. Settings > Preferences > Favorite Sections lets you hide or reorder entire sections on both Home and Favorites.

docs.title: 2.1.6 Notifications
docs.text: There are 3 types of notifications that can appear on the home page: 1. TV shows, anime or manga that got a new season or sequel found from background checks. 2. Calendar notifications for specific items that you manually enable on the calendar page. 3. System notifications that I manually make when I add an important update you should be informed about.

docs.title: 2.2 History Page
docs.text: Here you can see all your media items in one single place and you have more filtering options to search through them.

docs.title: 2.3 Calendar Page
docs.text: Here you can see all the past and upcoming releases displayed as pills inside a calendar. Pills older than 3 months are deleted automatically to not clutter the calendar or database for nothing. There is no limit for upcoming releases. The calendar automatically refreshes every time you access the page.

docs.title: 2.4 Favorites Page
docs.text:
Here you can see all your favorited items and reorder them. Choose small or big cards; in small mode, click to open an item or hold before dragging to reorder it. Your view choice is remembered in the browser.

The search bar matches media titles and creators, as well as person and character names. Empty sections are hidden while searching and reordering is disabled until you clear the search. Opening Favorites from a Home section puts that section first; otherwise your configured section order is used.

You can create custom people and characters using the + button if you can't find them through the APIs. Once a person or character is in your favorites, their page lets you assign media items from your library. Those links also appear on the assigned items' details pages.

docs.title: 2.5 Community Page
docs.text:
The community page uses a Realtime Database from Firebase to store data. It uses the free plan which from my calculations can support about 100 to 1000 users actively using the page every day. I didn't add user accounts so that the page is more likely to be used. This also means it can be easily abused and I am the only moderator. I just base my hopes that moderation won't be needed with a small number of users. If it ever gets out of control I can either add Firebase authentication or just nuke it :).

On the community page posts you can insert YouTube videos, Imgur images, links and media items (excluding custom items).

docs.title: 2.6 Collections Page
docs.text: Collections let you group items from different media types in one place. You can search the collections page by collection title, then search titles and creators inside a collection. Searching turns off reordering so filtered results don't accidentally change your saved order.

docs.title: 2.7 Settings
docs.text:
Preferences contains the theme, font and scoring options, along with a few ways to adjust what you see:

  • Navigation Buttons: Click to hide/show buttons and drag to reorder them. Favorites, Collections, History, Calendar, Discover and Community are available as extra buttons and start hidden. If seven or more buttons are enabled, the first five stay visible and the rest go into More.
  • Favorite Sections: Hide/show and reorder the media, People and Characters sections on Home and Favorites.
  • Live Search: Choose separately for each media type whether searching starts while you type.
  • List Card Overlays: Choose Full, Progress & Score or Hidden per media type. This affects card views; list views stay the same.
  • Banner Notes: Show or hide your item notes over the banner rotators on Home and list pages.
  • 18+ Content: Include or filter out provider-marked adult titles in search and Discover. This does not hide or remove items already saved in your library. It relies on the provider's classification, so it isn't a general filter for violence or mature themes.

docs.title: 2.7.1 Backups
docs.text:
Settings > Backup creates a ZIP archive containing your library database records and local media files. This includes settings, API keys, optional login accounts, collections, logs, people, screenshot records and music links. Use this when moving your installation or keeping a full backup, rather than CSV export.

Loading a backup checks the archive before restoring it. Uploading, validation and restoration have progress reporting, so a large library may spend some time validating before the item counter starts moving.

Browser-only choices, like player positions and view modes, stay in that browser rather than in the backup.

docs.title: 2.7.2 CSV Import and Export
docs.text:
Settings > Transfer lets you move media items and their personal fields between apps without needing a separate importer for each service. It is a one-time transfer, not continuous syncing. Use one row per item; JSON or XML exports need to be converted to a flat CSV first.

For importing, upload your file and choose what each column means. You can ignore columns you don't need, choose a media type for the whole file or map a type column, and match status values to the app's choices. Select the file's score scale and activity date format too. Decimal scores such as 2.5 and 2,5 are accepted; a decimal comma needs quotes if the CSV also uses commas between columns. Blank or zero scores mean unrated.

Provider IDs are the most reliable way to identify an item. AniList imports support both AniList and MyAnimeList IDs, and TV seasons can use Media Journal's show_id_sN TMDB ID format. Without IDs, the app searches by title and any mapped matching details such as year or creator. Review suggestions before pressing Import Matched Items. Search Again uses the title you enter and returns candidates for you to pick with Use This; it does not import them automatically.

Existing items are skipped without changing their notes, scores or dates. Rows that could not be imported can be downloaded with their original fields so you can correct them or add those items manually. Cancel on Match Columns clears the remembered import session and closes its panels.

Imports are limited to 50 MB and 50,000 rows per file. Matching and importing show progress and can be paused and resumed, including after a server restart. Temporary transfer data is cleaned up after seven days when a new transfer starts.

CSV exports contain personal fields, provider IDs, collection memberships and basic metadata. Scores use the internal 1–100 scale, with blank cells for unrated items. They do not include image files, people, logs or screenshot records. Formula-like text is protected for spreadsheets, and Media Journal restores its original text when re-importing its own export. The completed export message clears when you leave Settings.

docs.title: 2.7.3 Share Favorites
docs.text:
In Settings > Extras > Share Favorites, choose the sections you want to share, PNG or PDF, whether titles should appear and a maximum of 5, 10, 15, 20 or 25 items per section. The export follows your current theme and favorite item order, with a separate image or PDF page for each section.

For PNG, up to three sections download as separate images. Four or more are grouped into a ZIP. PDF puts the selected sections into one document. This is useful when you want to share your favorites without sharing a link to your private server.

docs.title: 2.8 Add to Your Home Screen
docs.text:
Open Media Journal through your own HTTPS address and choose Install app or Add to Home screen in your browser's menu. On iPhone, use Safari's Share > Add to Home Screen, with Open as Web App enabled if shown. The icon opens the app without the usual browser address bar.

No domain needs to be added to the app's code. It uses the address you installed from. Your server still needs to be running and reachable; offline use is not included. Regular HTTP access continues to work in the browser, but installation generally requires HTTPS, except for localhost on the same device.

If you use Tailscale, see Remote Access for a private HTTPS setup.

docs.title: YouTube "Video unavailable" Error
docs.text:
The Problem: When playing trailers or music within the app, you might encounter a black screen with the message: "Video unavailable, watch on YouTube."

The Cause: YouTube can block embedded playback for many popular videos when Media Journal is accessed through a numeric IP address, like http://192.168.1.15:8000 or http://127.0.0.1:8000. If many or most videos aren't playing, this is the first thing to check.

The Solutions: Use a named address instead of the numeric IP. Here are some options depending on your setup:

  1. Host Machine (Localhost): If you are on the same computer where the app is installed, simply use http://localhost:8000 instead of the IP address.

  2. Tailscale (Private Remote Access): If you use Tailscale to access the app across your devices, you can use your Tailscale machine name or MagicDNS URL instead of the IP address. (See Remote Access)

  3. Cloudflare Tunnels (Public Remote Access): A configured domain such as https://your-domain.com gives you a named HTTPS address for accessing the app. (See Remote Access)

  4. Local DNS: If you only want to fix this on your home network without exposing the app, you can set up a local DNS (either in your router settings or by running an app like Pi-hole). This allows you to assign a custom local name like http://mediajournal.local:8000.

Note: An individual video can also fail because it was deleted, made private or does not allow embedded playback.

docs.title: Music Pop-out Does Not Open
docs.text: Allow pop-ups for your Media Journal address, then try the pop-out control again. The player opens a separate browser window; it is not an always-on-top picture-in-picture window. Closing that window stops the player.

docs.title: CSV Rows Are Unmatched or Skipped
docs.text:
Check the selected media type, column mappings, score scale and date format. Provider IDs help avoid title ambiguity; AniList imports accept MyAnimeList IDs too. MusicBrainz IDs must identify recordings, and diary exports with repeated viewings need to be reduced to one row per item.

Search Again searches the title currently in its input. Replace a misspelled or fictional title with a real one, then choose Use This on a result. You still need to press Import Matched Items afterwards. An item already in your library is skipped and kept unchanged.

You can download the unimported CSV with the original fields for rows that need correcting. See CSV Import and Export for the full workflow.

docs.title: Home Screen Installation Is Missing
docs.text: Open your own HTTPS address rather than an HTTP IP address or machine name. If you use Tailscale, Tailscale Serve can provide this privately. On iPhone, use Safari's Share > Add to Home Screen. Installation options vary by browser, and the server must still be reachable after installation.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
By default Media Journal does not require a login to access. If you are hosting the app on a local network for personal use this is usually fine.

However, if you plan to expose the app to the internet (using a reverse proxy or Cloudflare Tunnels) it is highly recommended to enable authentication. This will lock down the entire app including your uploaded images and screenshots so only you can access them.

Setting up authentication is a two-step process: you must create an administrator account and then tell the app to require a login.

Note: This protects the same shared library. It does not create a separate media collection for each account.

docs.title: Step 1: Create an Account
docs.text:
Before you lock the app you need to create a "Superuser" account so you can actually log in.

DockerWindowsMacLinux

Open a terminal on the machine running your Docker container and run: 

docker exec -it media-journal python manage.py createsuperuser
It will prompt you to create a username, email (optional) and password. Note that as you type your password nothing will show on the screen for security reasons.

Open a terminal inside your media-journal folder and run: 

python manage.py createsuperuser
It will prompt you to create a username, email (optional) and password. Note that as you type your password nothing will show on the screen for security reasons.

Open your terminal, navigate to your media-journal folder, activate your virtual environment and run the command: 

source venv/bin/activate
python3 manage.py createsuperuser
It will prompt you to create a username, email (optional) and password. Note that as you type your password nothing will show on the screen for security reasons.

Open your terminal, navigate to your media-journal folder, activate your virtual environment and run the command: 

source venv/bin/activate
python manage.py createsuperuser
It will prompt you to create a username, email (optional) and password. Note that as you type your password nothing will show on the screen for security reasons.

docs.title: Step 2: Enable the Login Screen
docs.text:
Now that you have an account you need to start the app with the REQUIRE_LOGIN=True environment variable.

DockerWindowsMacLinux

Open your docker-compose.yml file and uncomment the REQUIRE_LOGIN line under the environment section: 

environment:
  - REQUIRE_LOGIN=True
Then restart your container to apply the changes: 
docker-compose down
docker-compose up -d

If using the .bat file (Recommended): Open your run_journal.bat file in a text editor and add set REQUIRE_LOGIN=True right before the runserver command: 

set REQUIRE_LOGIN=True
%PY% manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000 --noreload

If running manually in PowerShell: 

$env:REQUIRE_LOGIN="True"
python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000 --noreload

If running manually in CMD: 

set REQUIRE_LOGIN=True
python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000 --noreload

If using the Launchd Background Service (Recommended): Open your com.mediajournal.plist file in a text editor and add REQUIRE_LOGIN to the existing EnvironmentVariables dictionary. Keep TZ and any other keys already there; do not add a second dictionary. For example: 

<key>EnvironmentVariables</key>
<dict>
    <key>TZ</key>
    <string>Europe/London</string>
    <key>REQUIRE_LOGIN</key>
    <string>True</string>
</dict>
(Replace Europe/London with your local timezone.) Then restart the service in the terminal: 
launchctl unload ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.mediajournal.plist
launchctl load ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.mediajournal.plist

If running manually in the terminal: 

export REQUIRE_LOGIN=True
python3 manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000 --noreload

If using the Systemd Background Service (Recommended): Edit your service file (sudo nano /etc/systemd/system/mediajournal.service) and add Environment="REQUIRE_LOGIN=True" under the [Service] section: 

[Service]
Environment="REQUIRE_LOGIN=True"
User=YOUR_LINUX_USERNAME
Then restart the service: 
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart mediajournal

If running manually in the terminal: 

export REQUIRE_LOGIN=True
python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000 --noreload

docs.title: Remote Access
docs.text: To access Media Journal when away from home (for example, from a phone on cellular data) you have two main options.

docs.title: Option 1: The Private Way (Tailscale)
docs.text:
If you only need access for yourself this is the easiest and safest method.

You can use Tailscale, which is free for personal use. You install it on the machine running Media Journal and on your remote devices. It creates a direct, peer-to-peer encrypted tunnel between them.

  • Pros: Free, extremely secure, requires no domain configuration and the app does not need to be exposed to the public internet.
  • Cons: You must install Tailscale on every device you want to connect from. Also, if you use Private DNS on your Android phone (like AdGuard DNS), you may need to turn it off for the Tailscale address to work.

docs.title: HTTPS with Tailscale Serve
docs.text:
A plain http:// Tailscale address works for browsing, but home screen installation generally needs HTTPS. You can get a private HTTPS address without buying a domain by using Tailscale Serve.

  1. Start Media Journal normally, then open a terminal on the machine running both Media Journal and Tailscale.
  2. Run: 
    tailscale serve --bg http://127.0.0.1:8000
    For the default Docker setup, use http://127.0.0.1:8090 instead, since that is the port exposed on the host. If Tailscale asks you to enable HTTPS, follow the link it provides.
  3. Copy the HTTPS address shown by the command. It will look like https://your-device.your-tailnet.ts.net/. Add that origin to CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS using the instructions below, then restart Media Journal.
  4. Open that HTTPS address on your phone while connected to Tailscale. You can then add Media Journal to your home screen.

The --bg option keeps Serve configured across reboots. Media Journal and Tailscale still need to be running, and access remains private to your tailnet. To stop serving the HTTPS address, run:

tailscale serve --https=443 off

docs.title: Option 2: The Public Way (Cloudflare Tunnels)
docs.text:
To access the app from any web browser without installing a VPN app you must expose it to the internet. The modern standard for this is Cloudflare Tunnels using their Cloudflared application.

This requires a domain name. You can buy cheap promotional domains for around $1–$2 for the first year from registrars such as Porkbun, or look for platforms that give free subdomains. Some free subdomain services can take a long time to register or have limitations with Cloudflare.

Your domain needs to be configured with Cloudflare. Follow their Tunnel setup guide to connect your public hostname to the local Media Journal server.

  • Pros: The app is accessible instantly from any browser in the world via your custom URL.
  • Cons: Requires technical setup. You must also enable Authentication to prevent strangers from modifying your lists and accessing your data.

docs.title: Configuring the App for a Domain
docs.text:
When accessing the app through an HTTPS proxy, pages may load while login attempts or actions that save changes fail with a CSRF error. This can happen because Django receives HTTP traffic from the proxy while your browser uses an HTTPS address.

Set the CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS environment variable to your external origin, such as https://your-domain.com or your Tailscale HTTPS origin. Include the scheme and any non-default port, but leave out the trailing slash and page path. For multiple origins, separate them with commas.

DockerWindowsMacLinux

Open your docker-compose.yml file and uncomment the CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS line under the environment section. Ensure you include the https:// prefix. 

environment:
  - CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS=https://your-domain.com
(For multiple domains separate them with a comma).

Restart your container to apply the changes: 

docker-compose down
docker-compose up -d

If using the .bat file (Recommended): Open your run_journal.bat file in a text editor and add the variable right before the runserver command: 

set CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS=https://your-domain.com
%PY% manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000 --noreload

If running manually in PowerShell: 

$env:CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS="https://your-domain.com"
python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000 --noreload

If running manually in CMD: 

set CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS=https://your-domain.com
python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000 --noreload

If using the Launchd Background Service (Recommended): Open your com.mediajournal.plist file in a text editor and add it to your existing EnvironmentVariables dictionary. Keep any keys already there, such as TZ or REQUIRE_LOGIN, rather than adding a second dictionary: 

<key>EnvironmentVariables</key>
<dict>
    <key>CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS</key>
    <string>https://your-domain.com</string>
</dict>
Restart the service in the terminal: 
launchctl unload ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.mediajournal.plist
launchctl load ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.mediajournal.plist

If running manually in the terminal: 

export CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS=https://your-domain.com
python3 manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000 --noreload

If using the Systemd Background Service (Recommended): Edit your service file (sudo nano /etc/systemd/system/mediajournal.service) and add it under the [Service] section: 

[Service]
Environment="CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS=https://your-domain.com"
(If you already have REQUIRE_LOGIN=True configured you can separate them with a space: Environment="REQUIRE_LOGIN=True" "CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS=https://your-domain.com").

Restart the service: 

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl restart mediajournal

If running manually in the terminal: 

export CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS=https://your-domain.com
python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000 --noreload

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: This page outlines the technologies used to build Media Journal and how the codebase is structured.

docs.title: Tech Stack
docs.text:
Media Journal is built as a monolithic web application to keep self-hosting simple and reliable.

  • Backend: Django (Python 3.13)
  • Database: SQLite. It only allows one write at a time but because the app is meant for single-user or small family use it's good enough and doesn't require any extra database setup.
  • Frontend: Vanilla JavaScript, HTML and CSS
  • Database for the Community Page: Realtime Database from Firebase

docs.title: Minimal Dependencies
docs.text:
I intentionally keep the requirements as small as possible. I don't want to use external libraries unless they are truly needed. This is to future-proof the app so it doesn't depend on separate third-party packages that might break or get abandoned over time.

The main requirements.txt is extremely lightweight: 

Django==5.2.18
requests==2.32.3
whitenoise==6.11.0
waitress==3.0.2

For development the requirements-dev.txt includes the base requirements plus the documentation tools: 

-r requirements.txt
mkdocs-material==9.*
I use MkDocs for building this documentation and Ruff for general code checking and formatting.

docs.title: Production Serving
docs.text:
When users run the app natively (where debug mode is off by default) the app uses a couple of extra tools to run efficiently:

  • WhiteNoise: Used to serve static files (CSS, JS, images) directly through the Python web app so users don't have to set up a reverse proxy like Nginx.
  • Waitress: A production-quality WSGI server used to run the app on Windows, Linux and Mac instead of Django's default development server. Users can choose to use Waitress or the default runserver depending on what they need.

docs.title: External APIs
docs.text:
I use well-known free APIs that are more likely to last for years to come. The backend makes these requests, parses the JSON data and formats it before saving it locally.

  • TMDB: Movies and TV shows
  • AniList: Anime and Manga
  • IGDB: Games
  • OpenLibrary: Books
  • MusicBrainz & YouTube Search: Music

TMDB also supplies people, while AniList supplies characters and staff. Person URLs include the provider, such as /person/tmdb/123/ or /person/anilist/456/. Custom people use /person/custom/custom_.../, and characters use /character/123/. Old /person/actor/.../ and /person/character/.../ links still redirect to the current routes.

docs.title: Music Player and Home Screen Installation
docs.text:
The main app still uses normal Django page navigation. The in-page YouTube player reloads between pages, while /music/player/ runs it in a separate pop-out window so playback can continue. Player mode, position and pop-out size are saved in browser storage.

The web app manifest is generated at /manifest.webmanifest with relative app URLs, so each installation can use its own address. Home screen installation does not add offline caching or a service worker; the server must remain reachable.

docs.title: CSV Transfer
docs.text: The transfer views and services handle CSV upload, field and value mapping, provider matching, review and import/export progress. Jobs run in background threads, with staging data in data/transfer/ rather than new library models. Imports reuse the normal provider loaders with database writes deferred until an item is ready to save. No additional runtime dependency is needed.

docs.title: File Naming Conventions
docs.text:
To keep the codebase manageable without creating deeply nested folder structures I use a specific prefix naming convention. Files that belong to the same logical cluster share the same prefix across views, services, templates and static files.

  • g_ (General): Files used across multiple pages (e.g. g_base.html, g_edit_modal.js).
  • p_ (Page): Files specific to a standalone page (e.g. p_home.html, p_calendar.py, p_settings.css).
  • m_ (Media): Files for pages or functionalities that are mainly for media items (e.g. m_lists.js, m_games.html).

Because of this you can use the "Go to File" shortcut in Visual Studio Code (Ctrl + P or Cmd + P), type p_home and instantly see the HTML, CSS, JS and Python view files grouped together in the dropdown.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: If you want to contribute to the code, fix a bug or add a small feature you are more than welcome to do so. If you plan to make a big change or a major new feature please ask me first (like opening an issue) so you don't waste your time in case it's something I wouldn't merge.

docs.title: Branching Strategy
docs.text:
The repository has two main branches:

  • main: The stable release branch. This is what users download when they install the app.
  • development: The branch where I implement new things and test them before I merge them to the main branch.

Note: All Pull Requests should be made against the development branch. Once a set of features is stable I will merge them into main, draft a new release and make a new Docker image.

docs.title: Development Environment (DEBUG Mode)
docs.text:
In settings.py, debug mode is configured to read an environment variable: 

DEBUG = os.environ.get('MJ_DEV') == 'True'
This is done so that running the app normally on your machine defaults to DEBUG=False (production behavior), but when you open and run the app inside Visual Studio Code you automatically get DEBUG=True with live reload and detailed error pages.

To configure this in VS Code create a .vscode/settings.json file in the root folder of the project and add the MJ_DEV variable for your operating system:

WindowsMacLinux 
{
    "terminal.integrated.env.windows": {
        "MJ_DEV": "True"
    }
}

{
    "terminal.integrated.env.osx": {
        "MJ_DEV": "True"
    }
}

{
    "terminal.integrated.env.linux": {
        "MJ_DEV": "True"
    }
}

After saving the file any new terminal you open inside VS Code will automatically run with MJ_DEV=True.

docs.title: Database Schema
docs.text: The database is built using Django's ORM (the models.py file that maps Python code into the SQLite database). The goal is to keep a balance between tables and rows. Since the app tracks vastly different types of media I designed the database to minimize complex relational tables.

docs.title: The Unified MediaItem Model
docs.text:
Instead of creating separate tables for movies, books and games the app uses one unified table called MediaItem.

The media_type field dictates what the item is and the app renders it accordingly. To accommodate the different data structures required by different APIs the model heavily relies on JSONFields.

In cases for fields that refer to metadata (item data fetched from the API that won't change like cast, seasons and episodes) we use JSONFields. This avoids needing a dozen extra database tables just to store metadata and the data is saved exactly how we need to display it.

However for local data where we can have a massive amount of entries like game screenshots (which could reach thousands) or music URLs we make separate tables. Stuffing all of that into a single JSONField can slow down or break the database.

docs.title: Key Models Overview
docs.text:
• MediaItem: The core table. It stores all basic fields (title, cover, status, score) and uses a provider_ids JSON field to keep track of the item's ID from its respective API.
  • MediaItemLog: Handles the journal logs system. It links via a Foreign Key to a MediaItem and stores timestamped entries, progress updates and text logs.
  • Screenshot & MusicVideo: Separate tables linked to a MediaItem via Foreign Keys. They store individual game screenshots and YouTube music URLs so we don't overload the main item's JSON fields.
  • FavoritePerson: Stores people and characters from TMDB, AniList or custom entries. The source and person_id fields identify the provider and its ID together, so matching numbers from different APIs do not refer to the same person. The stored type='actor' value and media/favorites/actors/ folder are kept for compatibility, while the interface calls them People.
  • MediaPersonLink: Links a saved person or character to a media item, with an optional role for that specific item.
  • CalendarEvent: Links to a MediaItem to track release dates through calendar events. It handles both recurring rules and notification triggers.
  • Collection & CollectionItem: A Many-to-Many relationship structure that allows users to group various media items into custom lists.
  • AppSettings: A single-row table that stores user preferences like themes, scoring modes, details and favorite section ordering, per-type live search and card overlays, banner notes and adult content filtering.

docs.title: Backups and CSV Transfer
docs.text:
Full backups include the core models and their relationship tables, optional Django login accounts and groups, and files under media/. Restoring validates the archive before applying its database changes in a transaction. Scores and timestamps are preserved rather than going through the normal edit-item behavior.

CSV transfer has separate staging storage at data/transfer/state.sqlite3. Uploaded rows, mappings, match candidates and progress live there until they are imported or cleaned up. This keeps matching separate from the library database and allows a paused job to resume after a server restart. The directory is excluded from Git and Docker builds.

The importer prepares provider data before opening a short transaction for each new item, its related screenshot or music records and collection memberships. Existing items are kept unchanged. CSV export covers media items and their personal fields; use full backups for the rest of the library.

docs.title: Setup for Docker
docs.text:
New to Docker? If you haven't used Docker before and plan to run the app on your personal PC or laptop, check the other guides to set up the app natively without Docker.

  1. Clone the repository: 

    git clone https://github.com/mihail-pop/media-journal

  2. Open the docker-compose.yml file in a text editor, uncomment and update the TZ variable to your timezone. (Format is usually Continent/City like Europe/London or America/New_York. You can find a clean list of supported timezones here). Otherwise, it will default to UTC.

  3. Open a terminal in the project folder and start the app with: 

    docker-compose up -d
    The application will be available at http://localhost:8090.

  4. Inside the app, navigate to Settings → API Keys. You will need to add your own API keys. In that section there are instructions on how to obtain them.

docs.title: Remote Access
docs.text:
If you plan to use a tool like Cloudflare Tunnels to access the app remotely, you need to whitelist your domain name.

Open your docker-compose.yml file and uncomment the CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS line. Add your remote URL there: 

environment:  
  - CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS=https://your-domain.com
(Note: If you have multiple domains, you can separate them with a comma).

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
If you expose the app to the internet it is highly recommended to turn on authentication. You can enable this by uncommenting REQUIRE_LOGIN=True in your docker-compose.yml file.

To log in you will also need to create an administrator account (superuser).

Read the Authentication Guide

docs.title: Setup for Linux (Ubuntu/Debian)
docs.text:
1. Open your terminal and install Python, pip, virtual environment tools and Git: 

    sudo apt update
sudo apt install python3 python3-pip python3-venv git

  2. Navigate to the folder where you want the app installed and clone the repository: 

    git clone https://github.com/mihail-pop/media-journal
cd media-journal

  3. Create and activate a Virtual Environment: 

    python3 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate

  4. Install the dependencies: 

    pip install -r requirements.txt

  5. Create the database: 

    python manage.py migrate

  6. Generate static files (required after every update): 

    python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

  7. Start the app: 

    TZ=Europe/London python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000 --noreload
    Or use this command if you plan to run it on a machine 24/7: 
    TZ=Europe/London python -m waitress --listen=0.0.0.0:8000 --threads=8 media_journal.wsgi:application
    (Replace Europe/London with your local timezone. You can find a clean list of supported timezones here).

  8. Open the app in your browser at: http://localhost:8000

  9. Inside the app navigate to Settings → API Keys. You will need to add your own API keys. In that section there are instructions on how to obtain them.

docs.title: Access from Other Devices
docs.text:
To access the app from your phone, tablet or other devices on the same Wi-Fi network, use your computer's IP address instead of localhost.

You can find your IP address by running this command in the terminal: 

hostname -I
(Example: Once you find it, you would type http://192.168.1.15:8000 into your phone's browser).

docs.title: Run Automatically on Boot
docs.text:
To make the app start automatically and silently in the background when your Linux machine boots up, you can use Linux's built-in service manager called systemd.

1. Create the Service File: Open your terminal and create a new service file using the nano text editor: 

sudo nano /etc/systemd/system/mediajournal.service

2. Add the Configuration: Paste the following code into the terminal. Make sure to replace /PATH/TO/YOUR/ with the actual path to your folder and change YOUR_LINUX_USERNAME to your actual username. 

[Unit]
Description=Media Journal Waitress Server
After=network.target

[Service]
User=YOUR_LINUX_USERNAME
WorkingDirectory=/PATH/TO/YOUR/media-journal
# Replace Europe/London with your local timezone
Environment="TZ=Europe/London"
ExecStart=/PATH/TO/YOUR/media-journal/venv/bin/python -m waitress --listen=0.0.0.0:8000 --threads=8 media_journal.wsgi:application
Restart=always

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
(To save and exit nano: Press Ctrl+O, Enter, then Ctrl+X).

For timezone you can find a clean list of supported timezones here.

3. Activate the Service: Run these three commands to tell Linux to read your new file, start the app right now and enable it to start on every future boot: 

sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl start mediajournal
sudo systemctl enable mediajournal

If you want to access the app from outside your local Wi-Fi network, check the following guides:

Read the Remote Access Guide Read the Authentication Guide

docs.title: Setup for Mac
docs.text:
1. Download Python 3.13.0. Run the installer. (Note: After installation finishes, open your Applications folder, open the Python 3.13 folder and double-click Install Certificates.command. This ensures the app can safely connect to APIs).

  2. Open a terminal inside the folder where you want the app installed: Press Cmd + Space, type Terminal and press Enter. Type cd (with a space after it), drag the folder you want to use from Finder directly into the terminal window and press Enter.

  3. Clone the repository: 

    git clone https://github.com/mihail-pop/media-journal
    (Note: If you don't have Git installed, your Mac will automatically pop up a window asking to install "Command Line Developer Tools". Click Install, wait for it to finish and run the command again).

    Then navigate into the newly created folder: 

    cd media-journal

  4. Create and activate a Virtual Environment: (This keeps the app's dependencies separate from your other Python projects). 

    python3 -m venv venv
source venv/bin/activate

  5. Install the dependencies: 

    pip3 install -r requirements.txt

  6. Create the database: 

    python3 manage.py migrate

  7. Generate static files (required after every update): 

    python3 manage.py collectstatic --noinput

  8. Start the app: 

    TZ=Europe/London python3 manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000 --noreload
    Or use this command if you plan to run it on a machine 24/7: 
    TZ=Europe/London python3 -m waitress --listen=0.0.0.0:8000 --threads=8 media_journal.wsgi:application
    (Replace Europe/London with your local timezone. You can find a clean list of supported timezones here).

  9. Open the app in your browser at: http://localhost:8000

  10. Inside the app navigate to Settings → API Keys. You will need to add your own API keys. In that section there are instructions on how to obtain them.

docs.title: Access from Other Devices
docs.text:
To access the app from your phone, tablet or other devices on the same Wi-Fi network, use your Mac's IP address instead of localhost.

You can easily find your IP Address by holding down the Option (⌥) key and clicking the Wi-Fi icon in your top menu bar. Look for IP Address. (Example: Once you find it, you would type http://192.168.1.15:8000 into your phone's browser).

docs.title: Run Automatically on Startup
docs.text:
To make the app start automatically and silently in the background when you log into your Mac, you can use the built-in macOS service manager (launchd). No third-party apps are needed.

1. Create the Service File: Open a plain text editor (like TextEdit) and create a file called com.mediajournal.plist. Paste the following code into it, replacing /PATH/TO/YOUR/ with the actual path to your media-journal folder.

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<!DOCTYPE plist PUBLIC "-//Apple//DTD PLIST 1.0//EN" "http://www.apple.com/DTDs/PropertyList-1.0.dtd">
<plist version="1.0">
<dict>
    <key>Label</key>
    <string>com.mediajournal</string>
    <key>WorkingDirectory</key>
    <string>/PATH/TO/YOUR/media-journal</string>
    <key>EnvironmentVariables</key>
    <dict>
        <!-- Replace Europe/London with your local timezone -->
        <key>TZ</key>
        <string>Europe/London</string>
    </dict>
    <key>ProgramArguments</key>
    <array>
        <string>/PATH/TO/YOUR/media-journal/venv/bin/python3</string>
        <string>-m</string>
        <string>waitress</string>
        <string>--listen=0.0.0.0:8000</string>
        <string>--threads=8</string>
        <string>media_journal.wsgi:application</string>
    </array>
    <key>RunAtLoad</key>
    <true/>
</dict>
</plist>

For timezone you can find a clean list of supported timezones here.

2. Move the file to your hidden LaunchAgents folder: In Finder, press Cmd + Shift + G, type ~/Library/LaunchAgents/ and press Enter. Drag your com.mediajournal.plist file into this folder.

3. Activate the Service: Open Terminal and run this command: 

launchctl load ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.mediajournal.plist
The app will now run silently in the background every time you log in! (To stop it manually, run the same command but replace load with unload).

docs.title: Run Automatically on Boot
docs.text:
If you want the app to start before you log into your Mac, you can start it as a system service. You can do this by using the exact same .plist file from the previous step, but placing it in the System Daemon folder instead.

  1. Follow Step 1 above to create the .plist file.
  2. In Finder, press Cmd + Shift + G and go to /Library/LaunchDaemons/ (Notice there is no ~ at the start of this path!).
  3. Drag the .plist file into this folder. It will ask for your Mac admin password to confirm.
  4. Activate the background boot service by running this command in Terminal: 
    sudo launchctl load /Library/LaunchDaemons/com.mediajournal.plist

If you want to access the app from outside your local Wi-Fi network, check the following guides:

Read the Remote Access Guide Read the Authentication Guide

docs.title: Setup for Windows
docs.text:
1. Download Python 3.13.0. During installation check the option: “Add Python to PATH”.

  2. Open a terminal inside the folder where you want the app installed: Right-click inside your folder → Select Open in Terminal.

  3. Clone the repository (download GIT): 

    git clone https://github.com/mihail-pop/media-journal
    Then open a terminal in the newly created folder.

  4. Install the dependencies: 

    pip install -r requirements.txt

  5. Create the database: 

    python manage.py migrate

  6. Generate static files (required after every update): 

    python manage.py collectstatic --noinput

  7. Start the app: 

    python manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000 --noreload
    Or use this command if you plan to run it on a machine 24/7. 
    python -m waitress --listen=0.0.0.0:8000 --threads=8 media_journal.wsgi:application

  8. Open the app in your browser at: http://localhost:8000

  9. Inside the app navigate to Settings → API Keys. You will need to add your own API keys. In that section there are instructions on how to obtain them.

docs.title: Access from Other Devices
docs.text:
To access the app from your phone, tablet or other devices on the same Wi-Fi network, use your computer's IPv4 address instead of localhost.

You can find your IPv4 address by opening a terminal and running ipconfig. (Example: Once you find it, you would type http://192.168.1.15:8000 into your phone's browser).

docs.title: Run Automatically on Startup
docs.text:
To make the app start automatically in the background when you log into Windows, you can use a combination of a .bat file (to run the app) and a .vbs file (to hide the terminal window so it isn't in your way).

1. Create a .bat file (e.g., run_journal.bat) inside your project folder: 

@echo off  
cd /d "C:\***path to your folder***\media-journal"  
set PY="C:\***path to your python***\Python\Python313\python.exe"  
%PY% manage.py migrate  
%PY% manage.py collectstatic --noinput  
%PY% manage.py runserver 0.0.0.0:8000 --noreload

2. Create a .vbs file in your Windows Startup folder: (Press Win + R, type shell:startup and press Enter to open the folder). 

Set WshShell = CreateObject("WScript.Shell")  
WshShell.Run """C:\***path to your bat file***\run_journal.bat""", 0  
Set WshShell = Nothing

docs.title: Run Automatically on Boot
docs.text:
If you want the app to start before you log into Windows, you can start it as a service. You can do this by turning the .bat file from the previous step into a Windows service using NSSM. (The .vbs file won't be needed anymore).

  1. Open a terminal as Administrator and install NSSM: 

    winget install nssm

  2. Once installed, open a fresh Administrator terminal and run: 

    nssm install MediaJournal

  3. A graphical window will appear. In the Application tab, under Path, select the .bat file you created earlier.

  4. Go to the Log on tab, select This account and type in your Windows username and password.

  5. Click Install service.

  6. To start it immediately without restarting your PC, run: 

    nssm start MediaJournal

If you want to access the app from outside your local Wi-Fi network, check the following guides:

Read the Remote Access Guide Read the Authentication Guide
